cards.back: Pavement markings are lines painted on the road that guide and inform you without making you take your eyes off the roadway.
cards.front: What do pavement markings let you do while driving?

cards.back: In some places lines are made extra wide or fitted with reflective markers so they catch your attention and are easier to see.
cards.front: Why are some lines made extra wide or given reflective markers?

cards.back: Citing the National Highway Traffic Safety Administration, the manual says a crash where the limit is sixty-five miles per hour or more is over twice as likely to be fatal as one where the limit is forty-five or fifty miles per hour
cards.front: Compared with roads posted at forty-five or fifty, how much more likely is a fatal crash where the limit is sixty-five or more?

cards.back: The same NHTSA comparison says a crash on a road posted at sixty-five miles per hour or more is nearly five times as likely to be fatal as one on a road posted at forty miles per hour or less.
cards.front: Compared with roads posted at forty or less, how much more likely is a fatal crash on a road posted at sixty-five or more?

cards.back: According to the manual, no single step does more to keep you from being killed or badly hurt in a crash than wearing a seat belt, on every trip and in front or back seats.
cards.front: According to the manual, what single step does the most to keep you from being killed or badly hurt in a crash?

cards.back: About ninety percent of Maryland drivers and passengers buckle up, and the state's stated goal is one hundred percent.
cards.front: About what share of Maryland drivers and passengers buckle up?

cards.back: Buckling up takes about three seconds, and the manual says most injuries and deaths among unbelted crash victims could have been avoided by wearing a belt.
cards.front: About how long does buckling up take?

cards.back: The fatal-crash comparison grows with the gap in posted limits: over twice as deadly against roads posted at forty-five or fifty miles per hour, and nearly five times against roads posted at forty miles per hour or less.
cards.front: How does the fatal-crash comparison change with the gap in posted limits?

decks.module: why markings matter, speed and seat belt safety facts

cards.back: A single broken white line divides lanes carrying traffic the same way on roads with more than one lane, and you may cross it to change lanes.
cards.front: May you cross a single broken white line to change lanes?

cards.back: A single broken yellow line divides traffic moving in opposite directions and allows careful passing from either side; it serves as the center line on two-lane, two-way roads.
cards.front: What does a single broken yellow center line allow?

cards.back: A single solid white line marks the right edge of the road and can also divide same-direction lanes where changing lanes is discouraged.
cards.front: Between same-direction lanes, what does a single solid white line mean?

cards.back: Double solid white lines side by side divide same-direction lanes where lane changes are not allowed.
cards.front: What do double solid white lines between same-direction lanes mean?

cards.back: A broken white line lets you change lanes between same-direction lanes, a single solid white line discourages it, and double solid white lines prohibit it.
cards.front: How do broken white, single solid white and double solid white lines differ?
cards.memory_hook: Broken go, solid slow, double no

cards.back: A solid white line marks the right edge of a road, but a solid yellow line marks the left edge of divided highways, one-way roads and ramps.
cards.front: Which edge does a solid white line mark compared with a solid yellow line?

cards.back: A single broken yellow center line allows careful passing from both sides, while double solid yellow lines forbid passing from both sides.
cards.front: How does a broken yellow center line differ from double solid yellow lines?

decks.module: broken and solid white and yellow lines

cards.back: A single solid yellow line marks the left edge of divided highways, one-way roads and ramps.
cards.front: What does a single solid yellow line mark on divided highways, one-way roads and ramps?

cards.back: A divided highway is one with a guardrail, a strip of land or some other barrier between the two directions of traffic.
cards.front: What makes a highway a divided highway?

cards.back: Double solid white lines may also set general lanes apart from HOV lanes, or appear ahead of an obstruction you are allowed to pass on either side.
cards.front: What else may double solid white lines separate?

decks.module: left edge lines, divided highways and HOV separation

cards.back: Double broken yellow lines side by side mark the edges of a reversible lane, and you enter or leave that lane only as its signs and signals permit.
cards.front: What do double broken yellow lines side by side mark?

cards.back: Solid-plus-broken yellow lines also outline a two-way left turn lane, with the solid lines on the outside and the broken lines on the inside.
cards.front: How are the lines of a two-way left turn lane arranged?

cards.back: Double broken yellow lines outline a reversible lane, while solid outer lines with broken inner lines outline a two-way left turn lane.
cards.front: How do reversible-lane lines differ from two-way left turn lane lines?

decks.module: reversible lanes, two-way left turn lanes and dotted lines

cards.back: Double solid yellow lines divide opposing traffic and forbid passing from either direction.
cards.front: What do double solid yellow lines forbid?

cards.back: You are allowed to turn left across double solid yellow lines, for example to pull into a driveway.
cards.front: May you turn left across double solid yellow lines into a driveway?

cards.back: A solid yellow line beside a broken yellow line is used on two-way roads where passing is allowed in only one direction.
cards.front: Where is a solid yellow line beside a broken yellow line used?

cards.back: With a solid-plus-broken yellow pair, drivers on the broken-line side may pass carefully, while drivers on the solid-line side may not pass.
cards.front: With a solid-plus-broken yellow pair, which side may pass?

cards.back: With a solid line next to a broken yellow line, the rule depends on which line is nearer to you: broken on your side means you may pass with care, solid on your side means you may not.
cards.front: With a solid and a broken yellow line, what decides whether you may pass?

cards.back: Double solid yellow lines bar passing, yet a left turn across them, such as into a driveway, is still allowed.
cards.front: Double solid yellow bars passing. Does it also bar a left turn into a driveway?

decks.module: double solid yellow and solid-plus-broken yellow passing rules

cards.back: Word and symbol markings on the pavement tell you how to use a lane, which direction to travel, and when a lane reduction is coming, such as two lanes narrowing to one.
cards.front: What can word and symbol markings warn you about?

cards.back: Arrows and other word messages painted in a lane show how you are allowed to move from that lane.
cards.front: What do arrows painted in a lane show?

cards.back: SCHOOL and RxR painted on the road warn that you are nearing a school area or a railroad crossing.
cards.front: What do SCHOOL and RxR painted on the road warn of?

cards.back: A stop line is a solid white line showing where you must stop for a STOP sign or a red traffic signal.
cards.front: What does a stop line show?

cards.back: Yield lines are rows of small triangles painted across a lane that show where you must yield to vehicles or pedestrians.
cards.front: What do rows of small painted triangles across a lane show?

cards.back: Crosswalk lines are solid white lines marking where pedestrians cross, and some crosswalks add lines between them or use other lines instead.
cards.front: What color are crosswalk lines?

cards.back: A stop line is a single solid white line marking where to stop, while yield lines are rows of small triangles marking where to yield.
cards.front: How does a stop line differ from yield lines?

decks.module: stop lines, yield lines and crosswalks

cards.back: Most Maryland roads that bicycles share with motor vehicles carry no special signs or pavement markings for bicycles.
cards.front: Do most Maryland roads shared with bicycles have special bicycle markings?

cards.back: Shared-use lane markings, found mostly in cities, warn drivers that cyclists may be present, show cyclists where to ride, and discourage riding against traffic.
cards.front: Where are shared-use lane markings found mostly?

cards.back: Bicycle-only lanes are separated from motor vehicle lanes by solid or broken white lines and may be marked with bike lane signs or bicycle symbols and arrows.
cards.front: What separates bicycle-only lanes from motor vehicle lanes?

cards.back: Where parallel parking is permitted, similar lines may separate a bike lane from the parking lane.
cards.front: Where parallel parking is permitted, what may separate a bike lane from the parking lane?

cards.back: Shared-use lane markings mean cyclists and drivers share a lane, whereas a bike lane is set apart for bicycles by solid or broken white lines.
cards.front: How do shared-use lane markings differ from a bike lane?
